{{Short description|Optical illusion}}

[[File:the_disappearing_bicyclist_vanishing_puzzle.svg|thumb|upright|link={{filepath:the_disappearing_bicyclist_vanishing_puzzle.svg}}|Interactive SVG of ''The Disappearing Bicyclist'' &ndash; in [{{filepath:the_disappearing_bicyclist_vanishing_puzzle.svg}} the SVG file,] move the pointer to rotate the disc]]

A '''vanishing puzzle''' is a [[mechanical puzzle|mechanical]] [[optical illusion]] comprising multiple pieces which can be rearranged to show different versions of a picture depicting several objects, the number of which depending on the arrangement of the pieces.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bellos |first=Alex |author-link=Alex Bellos |date=2014-04-01 |title=Empire State Building vanishes: amazing images of geometrical illusion |language=en |work=The Guardian |url=http://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2014/apr/01/empire-state-building-images-geometrical-illusion-vanishing-leprechaun |access-date=2023-01-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2014-04-01 |title=Vanishing Leprechaun, Disappearing Dwarf and Swinging Sixties Pin-up Girls – puzzles in pictures |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/gallery/2014/apr/01/vanishing-leprechaun-disappearing-dwarf-puzzles-pictures |access-date=2023-01-15 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:the_magic_egg_puzzle.svg|thumb|Interactive SVG of ''The Magic Egg Puzzle'' &ndash; in [{{filepath:the_magic_egg_puzzle.svg}} the SVG file,] move the pointer to cycle its upper half]]
Wemple & Company marketed an advertising card named ''The Magic Egg Puzzle, (How Many Eggs?)'' in New York in 1880.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu/images/item.htm?id=http://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/lilly/slocum/LL-SLO-026561|title=Image Collections Online - "The Magic Egg Puzzle, (How Many Eggs?)"|website=webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu}}</ref>&nbsp;Cutting the rectangular card into four oblongs allowed the pieces to be rearranged to show either 8, 9 or 10 eggs. Many other similar puzzles have been published since.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.marianotomatis.it/blog/20110715|title=A selection of vanishing puzzles|website=Mariano Tomatis - Wonder Injector}}{{Dead link|date=February 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Chess player and recreational mathematician [[Sam Loyd]] patented rotary vanishing puzzles in 1896 and published versions named ''Get Off the Earth'', ''Teddy and the Lion'' and ''The Disappearing Bicyclist'' (pictured). Each had a circular card connected to a cardboard backdrop with a pin, letting it freely rotate.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7k1xYW18mQYC&pg=PA220|title=The Curious Book of Mind-boggling Teasers, Tricks, Puzzles & Games|first=Charles Barry|last=Townsend|date=January 8, 2003|publisher=Sterling Publishing Company, Inc.|isbn=9781402702143 |via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/puzzles-of-yore|title=Puzzles of Yore|website=Discover Magazine}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/02/23/the-disappearing-bicyclist/|title=The Disappearing Bicyclist: A Chess Champion's Vintage Puzzle to Tickle Your Brain|first=Maria|last=Popova|date=February 23, 2012}}</ref> In ''The Disappearing Bicyclist'', when the disc is rotated such that the arrow points to A, 13 boys can be counted, but when it points to B, there are only 12 boys.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu/images/item.htm?id=http://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/lilly/slocum/LL-SLO-025705|title=Image Collections Online - "The Disappearing Bicyclist!"|website=webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu}}</ref>
[[File:vanishing_puzzle_principle.svg|thumb|upright|Simplified rotary (left column) and sliding (right column) vanishing puzzles showing 2, 3 or 4 bars depending on the position of the moving part (yellow)]]

Prizes from $5 to $100 were offered for the best explanation of one illusion. Though the names of the winners were published, their explanations were not.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e04FEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA129 | title=Wheels, Life and Other Mathematical Amusements | isbn=9781470463625 | last1=Gardner | first1=Martin | date=1983| publisher=American Mathematical Soc. }}</ref>

==Similar puzzles==
The [[missing square puzzle]] is an [[optical illusion]] used in [[mathematics]] classes to help students reason about geometrical figures; or rather to teach them not to reason using figures, but to use only textual descriptions and the axioms of geometry. It depicts two arrangements made of similar shapes in slightly different configurations. Each apparently forms a 13×5 right-angled [[triangle]], but one has a 1×1 hole in it.
<gallery widths="160" heights="160">
Missing_square_puzzle-AB.svg|Both "total triangles" are in a perfect 13×5 grid; and both the "component triangles", the blue in a 5×2 grid and the red in an 8×3 grid
Loyd64-65-dis b.svg|[[Sam Loyd]]'s paradoxical dissection
Missing square edit.gif|A variant of Mitsunobu Matsuyama's "paradox"
</gallery>
[[Sam Loyd]]'s [[chessboard paradox]] demonstrates two rearrangements of an 8×8 square. In the "larger" rearrangement (the 5×13 rectangle in the image to the right), the gaps between the figures have a combined unit square more area than their square gaps counterparts, creating an illusion that the figures there take up more space than those in the original square figure.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://mathblag.wordpress.com/2011/08/28/a-paradoxical-dissection/|title=A Paradoxical Dissection|date=2011-08-28|work=mathblag|access-date=2018-04-19|language=en-US}} </ref>
